title: Egypt's Soccer Team Gets a Hero's Welcome After Their Best World Cup Ever!
summary: Imagine a sea of red, white, and black flags, drums beating, and fans singing at the top of their lungs. That was the scene in el-Alamein, Egypt, on Friday as the national soccer team came home from the World Cup. They didn't win the trophy, but they did something Egypt had never done before: they reached the last 16 teams! That's like making it to the quarterfinals of your school tournament for the very first time. Hundreds of supporters gathered at the airport, waving Egyptian and Palestinian flags. The players rode through the city on an open-top bus, smiling and waving. "We are very happy with the team," said fan Mohamed Gehad. "Their spirit was high, and ours is high as we welcome them." Egypt's journey was full of drama. They got their first-ever World Cup win and then beat Australia in a penalty shootout—a super tense way to decide a game where players kick from a spot 12 yards away. In the next match, they almost shocked the world. They were leading Argentina, the defending champions, 2-0 with only minutes left. But Argentina scored three quick goals and won 3-2. Even though they lost, fans were proud. They held signs saying, "You made us proud, men." Team captain Mohamed Salah, a famous forward who used to play for Liverpool in England, wrote on social media: "I'll do everything in my power to ensure this is a new beginning for Egyptian football on the international stage." Coach Hossam Hassan also made headlines by waving a Palestinian flag after the win over Australia. He said the suffering of people in Gaza was a "shame on the world." The team is set to meet Egypt's president on Saturday. Back in Gaza, many people had gathered in makeshift cafes—some made from salvaged metal—to watch Egypt's games. Sadly, a man who organized World Cup screenings there was killed in an airstrike earlier this week. The Egyptian Football Association also complained about the refereeing in the Argentina match, but FIFA's refereeing chief said the complaints were unfounded.
why_it_matters: Like a school sports team that tries its hardest even when it doesn't win, Egypt’s effort shows you can make your country proud just by never giving up.

FIFA (the world soccer organization that runs the World Cup) picks the host country and makes the rules. Mohamed Salah, Egypt’s captain, also plays for top clubs in Europe.
In Gaza, soccer brings people together even in hard times; many residents watched Egypt’s matches in simple cafés built from recycled materials.
